description:
We are a team passionate about curiosity, creativity, and innovation, united by the belief that exploration drives human progress.

Inspired by Ernst Stuhlinger's vision, we chose this challenge because protecting human health is one of space exploration's greatest challenges.

We hope our contribution will help advance space medicine and research into diseases like cancer, benefiting life on Earth.

“We explore to go further. We research to provide better care.”
summary:
EMMA is an Autonomous Space Health Node with integrated artificial intelligence and an offline-first architecture, designed to monitor and help protect astronauts' health without relying on a permanent connection to Earth.
Through an interactive dashboard, it integrates physiological, biomedical, and environmental variables associated with the five RIDGE risks: Radiation, Isolation, Distance, Gravity, and Environment, exploring their correlations and combined effects.
EMMA enables users to visualize trends, analyze changes in health indicators over time, and generate alerts. It includes 3D renderings of the liver and bones, along with a gamification system featuring challenges and rewards to encourage self-discipline and self-care.
We are presenting an MVP as a starting point for future developments in autonomous and personalized space medicine.
Because the future of space exploration depends not only on how far we can go, but also on our ability to care for those who take us there.
“We explore to go further. We research to provide better care.
details:
It is an Autonomous Space Health Node with an offline-first architecture, conceived as an intelligent and accesible platform for monitoring, analysis, and support for crew self-care. Through an interactive dashboard, it provides both an overall view and detailed views of each RIDGE risk category, tracking their evolution over time and their interrelationships. It also includes anatomical visualizations of the liver and skeletal system, along with a section for recommended actions.

The proposal combines ten core capabilities:

  1. Offline-first architecture and synchronization when connectivity is available: ensuring operational autonomy while maintaining system security, privacy, data integrity, and reliability.
  2. Integrated monitoring: bringing together physiological, biomedical, environmental, and behavioral information in a single platform.
  3. AI-powered contextual analysis: exploring relationships between variables, identifying patterns, and analyzing how they evolve over time.
  4. Alerts, prevention, and follow-up: highlighting relevant changes, trends, and potential risk situations that require attention.
  5. Interactive visualization: making information easier to understand through charts, indicators, and three-dimensional anatomical representations, using a visual, icon-based, and intuitive interface capable of presenting complex information without requiring advanced technical knowledge.
  6. Gamification and self-care: encouraging active crew participation through regular assessments, exercises, challenges, and rewards to promote motivation, consistency, and self-discipline.
  7. Data traceability: designed to maintain a signed record of data for validation, traceability, and use.
  8. Interactive mapping of space routes: by connecting with external measurement instruments and crew health monitoring systems, EMMA could provide relevant data to help contextualize and plan future space routes, taking health factors into account. This could also contribute to building a valuable database to help mitigate the risks and hazards of space exploration.
  9. Ensuring accessibility as a safety and functional measure: In space environments, quick access to information is essential. EMMA therefore includes a feature that adjusts the orientation of displayed information based on the detected position of the user's face and eyes. It responds to voice commands and provides spoken descriptions and narration in cases of visual impairment. It also recognizes users' native languages in cases of concussion or other injuries affecting cognitive function.
  10. Prioritization and Progressive Shutdown Protocol: EMMA is designed with a protocol that allows it to progressively reduce its functionalities according to their priority, adapting to the available energy and resource levels.
  11. Applications beyond space: remote monitoring, operational autonomy, preventive medicine, and integrated data interpretation could also be valuable in isolated environments, emergency situations, or locations with limited access to medical resources

Tools and Technologies

1. Interface (Crew Console and Ground Console)

  • React + TypeScript: both consoles, onboard and ground-based, with light-travel delay applied.
  • Vite: development server and frontend build tool.
  • Vitest: interface testing, including NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2, Appendix F requirements.
  • uPlot: real-time physiological time-series charts.
  • three.js: 3D scenes in the interface.
  • NiiVue: 3D viewer for reference medical volumes (CT/MRI), built on top of the Polaris viewer.
  • MediaPipe Tasks Vision: computer vision in the browser, without cloud services.
  • Vosk (vosk-browser): local speech recognition in the browser, without a network connection.
  • Web Bluetooth: direct connection to BLE wearables.
  • IBM Plex Sans / Mono: console typography, bundled locally (no remote fonts).

2. Server and Analysis

  • Python: backend programming language.
  • FastAPI + Uvicorn: API serving data, analysis, and recommendations to both consoles.
  • Pydantic / pydantic-settings: data validation and configuration (backend/.env, EMMA_ prefix).
  • NumPy, Pandas, SciPy: signal preprocessing, personal baselines, trends, and risk analysis.
  • SQLAlchemy + SQLite: append-only observation storage.
  • cryptography: integrity ledger, hash-chained and signed log.
  • httpx: HTTP client, always routed through the outbound traffic control in core/egress.py.

3. Health Data Standards

  • HL7 FHIR R4 (fhir.resources): canonical data model; all data enters as an Observation.
  • LOINC: verified codes for each indicator; other indicators use a justified custom coding system.
  • DICOM (pydicom): ultrasound image reading, calibration, and de-identification.
  • NIfTI (nibabel) + scikit-image: CT/MRI volumes and 3D meshes (marching cubes).

4. Desktop Application and Packaging

  • Electron: desktop application that starts the backend on loopback and opens the interface.
  • electron-builder (NSIS): Windows installer.
  • PyInstaller: packages the backend into an executable from a clean virtual environment.
  • bleak (optional): listens for BLE beacons inside the spacecraft.

5. Quality and Validation

  • pytest + respx (+ pytest-asyncio, pytest-cov): offline backend testing (respx mocks APIs), asynchronous tests, and code coverage.
  • Ruff + mypy --strict: linting and strict type checking.
  • Mutation testing campaigns: each safeguard has a test designed to deliberately break it.
  • Assistant benchmark (scripts/assistant_bench.py): measures the assistant's accuracy and latency when processing natural-language phrases, allowing comparisons between prompts, models, and routing strategies.
  • MMASH: real physiological data from healthy people on Earth; used to assess false alarms and sensitivity to simulated deterioration (does not validate space physiology).
  • LifeSnaps (Fitbit, Zenodo, CC BY 4.0): baseline validation.
  • HC18: guided ultrasound measurements.
  • TotalSegmentator Dataset (Zenodo, CC BY 4.0): sample medical volumes; Dice scores are measured only on test subjects.

6. Data and Wearables

  • Deterministic simulator: simulates in-flight physiology, with each parameter classified according to its supporting evidence.
  • Apple Health / Google Fit / BLE: data from real wearables.
  • CSV / JSON: downloaded datasets, tables, and samples included in the package.

7. Documents, Imaging, and Local AI (Entirely Cloud-Free)

  • Tesseract: local OCR for scanned reports.
  • pypdfium2, pypdf, ReportLab: PDF rasterization, reading, and generation.
  • Pillow: decodes image frames and serves them as PNG files.
  • Transformers + PyTorch + Hugging Face Hub (separate environment, optional): named entity recognition (NER) for report de-identification; the model is downloaded once, with its fingerprint verified.
  • Whisper + soundfile (separate environment, optional, CPU-based PyTorch): local speech transcription.
  • TotalSegmentator (separate environment, optional): organ segmentation in reference CT scans.
  • ONNX Runtime + tokenizers (e5-small model): local semantic search within the library.
  • Ollama (qwen3.5:9b): local language model for the natural-language assistant and draft interpretations (Class C, kept separate).

8. External APIs and NASA Sources

Space Environment

  • JPL Horizons (https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov, via astroquery.jplhorizons): ephemerides for calculating Earth-to-spacecraft light-travel time.
  • NAIF SPICE (https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov, spiceypy, optional): kernels are downloaded once, allowing light-travel time and solar elongation to be calculated locally, without a network connection.
  • NASA DONKI (https://api.nasa.gov): space weather events.
  • CCMC iSWA (https://iswa.gsfc.nasa.gov, HAPI, no API key required): proton and solar wind time series.
  • SSCweb (https://sscweb.gsfc.nasa.gov): ISS position for the low Earth orbit profile.
  • RadLab / DosTel (https://visualization.osdr.nasa.gov): radiation doses measured during spaceflight.

Evidence Supporting Recommendations

  • NASA OSDR (https://visualization.osdr.nasa.gov): records of cited studies; only the public study identifier is displayed (OSD-288…).
  • NASA Human Research Program (HRP): program risks and supporting evidence; linked as references rather than accessed through an API.
  • NASA NTRS (https://ntrs.nasa.gov): technical reports identified by report number.
  • Crossref, DataCite, and doi.org: verification of citation existence and DOI resolution.
  • PubMed (NCBI E-utilities) and ClinicalTrials.gov: cited scientific articles and clinical trials.

9. Third-Party Code Adopted

  • Polaris: clinical tools and 3D viewer, copied directly (AGPL-3.0). The original repository has since been made private again: https://github.com/BeyondTheProtocol/polaris. A new public version with differences is available at https://github.com/BeyondTheProtocol. We have authorization from the author, Miriam Gonzalez, @miriamgonp.
  • Marplanner (Node.js): routine and task planner, running as a local loopback service (MIT). Its technology stack includes Fastify, Drizzle ORM + better-sqlite3, Zod, Schedule-X (calendar), Radix UI, and Tailwind. (MIT) https://github.com/diegomarino/marplanner.
  • planner-bridge (Node.js): our own bridge between Marplanner and EMMA; sends its records to the ledger and routes its outbound internet traffic through the same egress control. (AGPL-3.0) https://github.com/JetBrains/JetBrainsMono.
  • qwen3.5:9b (Ollama): Natural-language assistant: identifies the user's intent and generates the response (Apache-2.0). https://ollama.com/
  • gemma4 (Ollama): Drafts interpretations (Class C, kept separate). Transcribes the assistant's voice input when the model supports audio input (Apache-2.0). https://ollama.com/
  • gemma4:12b-it-qat (Llama): Sole verifier of interpretation drafts (Apache-2.0) https://ollama.com/
  • Whisper base (OpenAI): Speech-to-text when the model does not support audio input (MIT). https://ollama.com/
  • multilingual-e5-small: Local semantic search within the library (MIT). https://ollama.com/
  • MediaPipe Face Landmarker: Facial tracking through the camera (Apache-2.0).
  • Vosk small-es-0.42: Assistant wake-word detection (Apache-2.0). https://ollama.com/
  • TotalSegmentator: Organ segmentation in reference CT scans (free-weight tasks only) (Apache-2.0). https://github.com/BeyondTheProtocol/polaris. A new public version with differences is available at https://github.com/BeyondTheProtocol. We have authorization from the author, Miriam Gonzalez, @miriamgonp.
